title: Number of Islands
prompt: Given an m x n 2D grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands. An island is a maximal group of land cells connected 4-directionally (up, down, left, right). Cells connected only diagonally are NOT part of the same island. The grid's borders are all surrounded by water.
blurb: Counting connected components on a grid — flood-fill each unvisited land cell with DFS/BFS, or union adjacent land with union-find.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Confirms 4-directional (not 8) connectivity, asks whether the grid may be mutated, and whether it can be huge (which motivates BFS over deep recursion).

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Frames it as counting connected components: scan cells, and on each unvisited land cell increment the count and flood-fill (DFS or BFS) the whole component. Can articulate the union-find alternative.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Marks cells visited (sink to '0' or a visited set) so a component is counted exactly once; bounds-checks the four neighbors; never revisits; only counts land.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(m*n) time — each cell is visited a constant number of times. Space O(m*n) worst case for the DFS recursion stack / BFS queue (a grid that is all land), or O(m*n) for union-find structures.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: A clean neighbor iteration (direction array), a single flood-fill helper, and a guard that merges bounds + water + visited checks at the top of the recursion/pop.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty grid, all water (0), all land (1), single cell, single row/column, diagonal-only touching land (still separate islands), a large all-land grid causing recursion depth concerns.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests the diagonal-adjacency trap and an all-land grid; verifies the count, not just that it runs.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Names it as connected components, states the visited strategy explicitly, and discusses the recursion-depth risk for very large grids.

examples.explanation: The top-left 2x2 block is one island; the two lone land cells at (2,2) and (3,3) are two more. (2,2) and (3,3) touch only diagonally, so they are separate.
All land cells are connected 4-directionally through the middle column and row, forming a single island.

test_cases.expected: 3 — single row, three separated land cells
2 — diagonal-only touch counts as two islands, NOT one
1 — stresses recursion depth; a naive DFS may overflow the stack, motivating BFS or an explicit stack

reference.optimal_space: O(m*n) worst case (recursion stack / BFS queue / union-find arrays); O(min(m,n)) for BFS on the frontier in the best analysis

approaches.name: DFS flood-fill
approaches.idea: Scan every cell. When you hit a '1', increment the island count and recursively DFS its 4 neighbors, sinking each visited land cell to '0' (or marking a visited set) so it isn't counted again. Simple and fast, but recursion depth can reach m*n on an all-land grid and blow the stack.

approaches.name: BFS flood-fill
approaches.idea: Same scan, but flood each component with an explicit queue instead of recursion: on an unvisited '1', enqueue it, mark it water, and BFS outward marking neighbors as they are enqueued. Avoids deep recursion — preferred for very large grids.

approaches.name: union-find (disjoint set)
approaches.idea: Give each land cell an id. Union each land cell with its right and down land neighbors (two directions suffice to cover all adjacencies). The answer is the number of distinct roots among land cells. With path compression + union by rank it is near-linear; natural fit if edges arrive incrementally (see the streaming follow-up).

follow_ups: Max Area of Island — return the size of the largest component instead of the count (flood-fill returns a size).

Number of Islands II (streaming) — land cells are added one at a time; after each addition report the current island count. Union-find shines here: each addLand unions with existing land neighbors and adjusts a running count.
Count without mutating the input — use a separate visited matrix or restore cells afterward.
8-directional connectivity (include diagonals) — extend the neighbor set to 8; discuss how it changes the examples.
Islands that touch the border don't count / surrounded regions (flood-fill from the border first) — the complement pattern.
reference.reference_solution:
numIslands(grid): if grid is empty: return 0. m, n = dims; count = 0. for i in range(m): for j in range(n): if grid[i][j] == '1': count += 1; dfs(grid, i, j). return count.

dfs(grid, i, j): if i < 0 or i >= m or j < 0 or j >= n or grid[i][j] != '1': return  // bounds + water + visited all in one guard. grid[i][j] = '0'  // sink so it is never revisited. for (di, dj) in [(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)]: dfs(grid, i+di, j+dj).

Sinking to '0' doubles as the visited marker, so no extra matrix is needed if mutation is allowed. For an all-land 300x300 grid the recursion can nest 90000 deep — switch to an explicit stack or BFS queue to stay safe. Union-find alternative: init parent[cell]=cell for land; for each land cell union with its right and down land neighbors; answer = number of unique find() roots.
pitfalls: Not marking cells visited, so a single island is counted many times or the DFS loops forever.
Counting 8-directional adjacency when the problem says 4-directional (or vice versa) — clarify first.
Missing bounds checks before indexing a neighbor (index out of range on edges/corners).
Deep recursion stack overflow on a large all-land grid — use BFS or an explicit stack.
Mutating the grid when the caller needed it preserved — use a visited set instead.

interviewer_notes: Most candidates reach DFS flood-fill quickly; the mid-level signal is a clean visited strategy and correct bounds checks. First clarifying signal: do they confirm 4- vs 8-directional? If not, let them assume 4 and later challenge with [[1,0],[0,1]] during testing. Stay silent through the flood-fill; nudge only if they forget to mark visited (their island count will explode — hand them a 2x2 all-land grid and ask for the count). The senior escalation is Number of Islands II (streaming adds): this is where union-find becomes clearly superior to re-running flood-fill after each insert, and a strong candidate reaches for it unprompted. If they used recursion, ask what happens on a 300x300 all-land grid to surface the stack-depth issue and see if they can convert to BFS.
